speaker: John Quinn
title: Ep 110 | John B. Quinn | Big Law Litigation Trailblazer & Pioneer
question: In a jury trial, how can visible nervousness in an inexperienced trial lawyer actually affect the courtroom dynamic?
guest: You can get over it. But as I look back on it, from the standpoint of my opposing counsel and the jury, to see a young person up there shaking and nervous—that's not a bad message in a way. Some jurors are going to be pulling for you. Afterwards we talked to some of the jurors—that trial ended up being three months—and one of the jurors told me, 'You came a long way in that trial.' They saw me personally developing. So now, think about when I'm in a jury trial: I'm an older gray-haired guy who's obviously been around the block, and if my opponent on the other side is a young woman who's clearly nervous and trying to make it, I think I'm at a disadvantage. If you're on that jury, who are you going to pull for?

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Visible nervousness cuts both ways, and its effect depends largely on how the lawyer handles it.

On the downside, jurors often read confidence as a proxy for credibility. A lawyer who fumbles exhibits, speaks haltingly, or avoids eye contact can lead jurors to infer that the lawyer doubts their own case. Nervousness also distracts: jurors may watch the lawyer's discomfort rather than absorb the evidence. It can embolden opposing counsel to object more aggressively and may make witnesses harder to control on cross-examination.

On the upside, trial advocacy teachers have long observed that jurors tend to sympathize with an obviously inexperienced lawyer, especially one facing a polished, aggressive opponent. Nervousness can read as sincerity and humanity, and an underdog dynamic may develop. If opposing counsel bullies the novice, jurors often resent it. Judges sometimes extend a little procedural patience as well.

The key variable is preparation and candor. A nervous but well-prepared, earnest lawyer usually keeps the jury's goodwill, while nervousness combined with disorganization erodes it. Either way, jurors are instructed to decide on the evidence, and strong facts generally matter more than delivery.

Visible nervousness in an inexperienced trial lawyer creates a complex, double-edged shift in courtroom dynamics. With jurors, mild anxiety often humanizes counsel; because laypeople find courtrooms intimidating themselves, a slightly nervous, earnest attorney can seem authentic and relatable, sometimes generating underdog sympathy against a slick or overbearing opponent. However, if nerves escalate into fumbling exhibits, speaking too fast, or losing one's train of thought, jurors grow distracted from the evidence and may subconsciously read that unease as a lack of faith in the client's case.

Beyond the jury box, visible tension reshapes how other courtroom participants behave. Friendly witnesses frequently mirror their lawyer's anxiety on the stand, while adverse witnesses may sense hesitation during cross-examination and become more evasive. Seasoned opposing counsel may test an unsteady advocate with rapid objections to disrupt their rhythm, though bullying a nervous newcomer risks alienating the jury. Meanwhile, judges may either offer measured leeway to ensure a fair trial or grow impatient if disorganization slows proceedings.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Visible nervousness changes the courtroom in two directions, and which one wins depends mostly on how the lawyer handles it.

The downside is credibility. Jurors watch lawyers closely, and fidgeting, a shaky voice or fumbling with exhibits can come across as doubt about the case. Jurors may then discount the arguments or look more to the opposing counsel who seems calmer. Nerves also cause practical mistakes: missed objections, rigid reliance on a script, poor listening during cross-examination and lost momentum. Experienced opponents and judges notice this and may push harder, and a judge may step in more often to keep things moving.

The upside is that jurors often find a nervous lawyer sincere and relatable, especially next to a polished, aggressive opponent. That can make the opponent look slick and draw some sympathy toward the nervous lawyer's client. Jurors also tend to forgive nerves at the start, so a lawyer who settles down can still win their trust.

In the end, jurors care less about whether a lawyer is nervous than about whether they seem prepared, honest and respectful. Careful preparation, a clear theme and composure that recovers over the trial usually matter much more than early jitters.
